Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Football Why EPL talents struggle to replicate club brilliance at Black Stars level Source : Salihu Shuaib Jaarah 21 October 2026 7:52am Antoine Semenyo Audio By Carbonatix
Ghana possesses some of the most exciting attacking talents in English football, but translating individual brilliance into consistent performances for the Black Stars remains a challenge worth examining.
Antoine Semenyo, Mohammed Kudus and Abdul Fatawu Issahaku have demonstrated their ability to dribble paas defenders, create goal scoring opportunities and influence matches at club level.
Yet questions persist about whether Ghana’s tactical approach, team structure and attacking combinations are allowing these players to deliver their potential to the highest level on the international stage.
The issue is not necessarily a lack of quality or commitment from the players. Instead, it raises a broader question: is Ghana doing enough to create the conditions in which its most talented attackers can thrive?
One of the biggest differences between club and international football is the tactical system in which players operate.
At club level, players train regularly under the same coach, learn specific attacking patterns and develop a clear understanding of their responsibilities. They often know when to make runs, where to receive the ball and how their teammates will link up play.
For Semenyo, whose pace, strength, direct running and ability to cut inside make him a dangerous attacking threat, positioning is particularly important. If he receives the ball in advanced areas with space to attack defenders, he can use his qualities to create a goal scoring opportunities.
However, deploying him in unfamiliar positions or asking him to perform several different roles can disrupt his rhythm.
Ghana’s 1-0 victory over Panama in the opening match of the 2026 FIFA World Cup offered a typical example. Tactical analysis of the game noted that Semenyo moved between the wing and a more central attacking role before finding greater success with freedom to drift inside. He was subsequently named Player of the Match.
The lesson is not that Semenyo cannot adapt, but that Ghana must identify the positions and combinations that best exploit his strengths.
Even the most talented attacker needs support from his teammates.
At their clubs, Semenyo, Kudus and Fatawu benefit from established passing patterns, coordinated movements and players who understand when to provide support. These relationships help them receive the ball in dangerous areas rather than having to create every opportunity on their own.
For Ghana, the challenge is to ensure that the midfield can progress the ball effectively and that the forwards are not left isolated against several defenders.
When passes arrive too slowly, attacking runs go unnoticed or overlapping support is missing, opponents have more time to organise their defensive shape.
Wingers who thrive in one-on-one situations can suddenly find themselves facing two or three defenders with limited options.
This makes the quality of service just as important as the individual ability of the player receiving the ball.
If the Black Stars want their attacking talents to make a greater impact, the team must create more opportunities for them to receive possession in positions where they can threaten the opposition goal.
Although Semenyo, Kudus and Fatawu are often discussed together, they are not identical players. Each offers a different set of qualities, and Ghana must recognise those differences when developing its attacking system.
Semenyo is a powerful, direct forward capable of carrying the ball at speed, taking on defenders and finishing chances. His game benefits from space, quick transitions and the freedom to attack from wide areas.
Kudus offers close control, strength in possession, dribbling ability and the capacity to carry the ball through tight spaces. He can influence a match by creating opportunities for himself or drawing defenders away from teammates.
Giving him opportunities to receive the ball between the opposition’s midfield and defensive lines can help maximise his creativity.
Fatawu, meanwhile, brings pace, left-footed delivery, direct running and the willingness to take on defenders from wide positions. He can stretch defensive lines, deliver crosses and cut inside to create shooting opportunities.
The coaching challenge is to build combinations that allow these qualities to complement one another rather than placing all three players in situations where they are expected to produce individual moments of magic.
A well-structured attack should give each player a defined role while allowing enough freedom for improvisation when opportunities arise.
Club football offers players considerably more time to develop team chemistry than international football does.
At their clubs, attackers work together throughout the season. They become familiar with each other’s movements, preferred passing angles and decision-making. Such understanding often makes the difference between a promising attack and a clear scoring opportunity.
The Black Stars, by contrast, assemble for relatively short international windows. Players arrive from different leagues and tactical systems, leaving coaches with limited time to develop consistent patterns of play.
This can affect the timing of attacking runs, the quality of combinations around the penalty area and the team's ability to react quickly when possession changes.
However, limited preparation time should not become a permanent excuse. Clear tactical principles, consistent player roles and well-rehearsed set-piece routines can help a national team build cohesion despite the restrictions.
Ghana must find ways to make its attacking play more coordinated, particularly when facing opponents who defend in compact formations with tight spaces for individual dribbling.
The growing reputation of Ghanaian players in English football has raised expectations among supporters.
When Semenyo, Kudus or Fatawu delivers an outstanding performance for their clubs, fans naturally expect similar displays in the Black Stars jersey. When those performances fail to materialise, criticism often focuses on the players themselves.
But individual statistics do not always tell the full story. Goals, assists and successful dribbles depend partly on a team's tactical structure, the quality of opposition and the opportunities created during a match.
It would therefore be unfair to conclude that a player is underperforming solely because his national-team numbers do not match his club statistics. Each performance must be assessed in context, including his position, fitness, responsibilities and the quality of chances available to him.
At the same time, playing for Ghana carries its own responsibilities. The players must find ways to adapt to different conditions, make better decisions under pressure and contribute to the collective effort even when the team is struggling.
The objective should be to balance accountability with a fair assessment of the circumstances surrounding their performances.
Perhaps the most important question is whether the Black Stars have developed a reliable attacking identity.
When a team consistently depends on its most talented players to produce moments of individual brilliance, it risks becoming predictable. Opponents can focus their defensive attention on those players, close down their preferred spaces and force other members of the team to take responsibility.
Ghana needs an attacking structure that creates opportunities through collective movement, intelligent positioning and quick combinations.
The objective should not be to make Semenyo, Kudus and Fatawu less influential, but to ensure that their individual abilities are supported by a functioning team.
The national team must also develop alternative ways of creating chances when its wide attackers are tightly marked. Better movement from central midfielders, overlapping full-backs and more effective combinations around the penalty area could help reduce the burden on the three players.
Ultimately, individual quality becomes more effective when it is supported by collective organisation.
Ghana’s challenge is not simply about having players capable of competing at the highest level. It is about creating a national-team structure that consistently brings out their best qualities.
Semenyo, Kudus and Fatawu have different strengths, and expecting them to reproduce their club performances without considering the differences in tactics, teammates and responsibilities would be an oversimplification.
The Black Stars' coaching staff must establish clear attacking roles, improve the connection between midfield and attack, and create the conditions for these players to receive the ball in dangerous areas. The players, in turn, must adapt to the demands of international football and demonstrate that their individual qualities can serve the collective objective.
For Ghana, the real measure of success is not whether its Premier League talents can reproduce every club-level statistic in a Black Stars shirt. It is whether the team can build a system in which their abilities consistently translate into goals, chances created and meaningful contributions to winning matches.
The question Ghana must answer is simple: does the Black Stars have a problem with its players, or has it yet to find the right system to unlock them?
